title: Euler's Totient mod 4: A Corrected Characterization of $\varphi(n)\equiv 2\pmod 4$
description: Answers the mod-4 refinement open question of the parent `euler-totient-oq-06` (its openQuestions[1]): characterize exactly which n satisfy φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4), equivalently v₂(φ(n)) = 1. Writing n = 2^a·m with m odd, Euler's product formula gives the additive split v₂(φ(n)) = (a − 1) + Σ_{p ∣ m} v₂(p − 1), where each odd prime p ∣ m contributes v₂(p − 1) ≥ 1. For the total to equal 1 there are TWO families of solutions: (i) a ≤ 1 with a single odd prime factor p ≡ 3 (mod 4), giving n = p^k or n = 2p^k; and (ii) a = 2 with no odd prime factor, i.e. n = 4. The last case is easy to miss — φ(4) = 2 ≡ 2 (mod 4), yet 4 is neither p^k nor 2p^k for an odd prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) — so the naive characterization 'n = p^k or 2p^k' (as sketched in the parent) is incomplete; the theorem `four_is_extra_solution` records n = 4 as an explicit counterexample. The proof reuses the sibling oq-01 machinery (the 2-adic valuation master formula) and adds the finite sum-analysis needed to pin down v₂(φ(n)) = 1. Fully machine-checked: 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

mathlibDependencies.description: `n ≠ 0 → φ n = n.factorization.prod (fun p k => p^(k-1)·(p-1))`. Euler's product formula, the source of the additive-over-primes structure of v₂(φ(n)).
`p.Prime → 0 < n → φ (p^n) = p^(n-1)·(p-1)`. Gives the prime-power building blocks v₂(φ(2^a)) = a−1 and v₂(φ(p^k)) = v₂(p−1).
`a ≠ 0 → (p^n ∣ a ↔ n ≤ padicValNat p a)`. The bridge between divisibility by powers of 2 and the 2-adic valuation, used to prove v₂(m) = 1 ↔ m ≡ 2 (mod 4).
`a ≠ 0 → b ≠ 0 → padicValNat p (a·b) = padicValNat p a + padicValNat p b`. Additivity of the valuation over products, applied to the 2-part / odd-part split φ(n) = φ(2^a)·φ(m).
`ordProj[p] n · ordCompl[p] n = n`, i.e. n = 2^(v₂ n) · (odd part). With `coprime_ordCompl` and `not_dvd_ordCompl` this realizes the 2-part / odd-part decomposition and its coprimality.
`IsPrimePow n ↔ n.primeFactors.card = 1`. Reconstructs 'the odd part has a single prime factor' into the concrete form m = p^k needed for the characterization.

originalContributions: `v2_totient_eq_one_iff`: the corrected biconditional characterization of v₂(φ(n)) = 1, exhibiting the THREE solution families n = 4, n = p^k, and n = 2p^k (odd prime p ≡ 3 mod 4, k ≥ 1) — answering the parent's openQuestions[1].

`four_is_extra_solution`: an explicit proof that n = 4 satisfies φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) yet is neither p^k nor 2p^k for an odd prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4), showing the naive characterization is incomplete. This is the mathematical correction at the heart of the entry.
`v2_totient_master`: the 2-part / odd-part split v₂(φ n) = (v₂(n) − 1) + Σ_{p ∣ oddpart} v₂(p − 1), a self-contained re-derivation isolating the prime 2 that drives the whole analysis.
`padicValNat_two_eq_one_iff`: the reusable arithmetic core v₂(m) = 1 ↔ m ≡ 2 (mod 4) for every natural m, which turns the mod-4 question into a valuation question.
`totient_mod_four_eq_two_iff`: the direct mod-4 restatement φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) ↔ (the three families), the form matching the parent's open question verbatim.

The 2-part / odd-part decomposition n = 2^(v₂ n) · (odd part)

relatedProblems.relationship: Direct parent: settles the parity of φ (even for n > 2). This entry answers its openQuestions[1] — the mod-4 refinement — and corrects the parent's sketched characterization by exhibiting n = 4 as an extra solution.

overview.historicalContext: After Euler introduced φ(n) = |(ℤ/nℤ)ˣ| in his 1763 generalization of Fermat's little theorem, the parity fact 'φ(n) is even for n > 2' became a staple (the parent entry euler-totient-oq-06). The natural next question — refining parity to residues mod 4 — asks precisely when φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4), equivalently when the 2-Sylow subgroup of (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ has order exactly 2. Because φ is multiplicative and φ(p^k) = p^(k−1)(p−1), the 2-adic valuation v₂(φ(n)) is a sum of local contributions, one per prime factor of n; the mod-4 question is the first place where the interaction between the odd primes p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and the power of 2 dividing n becomes visible.
overview.problemStatement: **Open Question (euler-totient-oq-06, openQuestions[1]):** characterize when φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) versus ≡ 0 (mod 4). Equivalently, determine all n with v₂(φ(n)) = 1.
overview.text: φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) holds exactly for n = 4, for n = p^k, and for n = 2p^k, where p is an odd prime with p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k ≥ 1. The case n = 4 is a genuine extra solution that the naive characterization 'n = p^k or 2p^k' omits.
overview.proofStrategy: First reduce the mod-4 question to a valuation question: for every m, v₂(m) = 1 ↔ m ≡ 2 (mod 4) (`padicValNat_two_eq_one_iff`, via `padicValNat_dvd_iff_le` bounding v₂ between the divisibilities 2 ∣ m and 4 ∤ m). Next establish the prime-power building blocks v₂(φ(2^a)) = a − 1 and, for odd primes, v₂(φ(p^k)) = v₂(p − 1) with v₂(p − 1) = 1 ↔ p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Decompose n = 2^a·m (m odd) using ordProj/ordCompl and multiplicativity to get the master split v₂(φ n) = (a − 1) + Σ_{p ∣ m} v₂(p − 1). Since every odd-prime summand is ≥ 1, a sum equal to 1 forces at most one odd prime; a finite case analysis on a (≤ 1, = 2, ≥ 3) then yields the three families, reconstructing m = p^k from 'single prime factor' via IsPrimePow.
keyInsights: **The mod-4 question IS a 2-adic valuation question.** φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) is literally v₂(φ(n)) = 1; `padicValNat_two_eq_one_iff` makes this equivalence precise for every natural number, so all subsequent work is about a single integer, the valuation.

**Additivity localizes the problem.** Because v₂ is additive over products and φ is multiplicative, v₂(φ(n)) = (v₂(n) − 1) + Σ_{odd p ∣ n} v₂(p − 1): each odd prime factor p contributes v₂(p − 1) ≥ 1, and the power of 2 contributes v₂(n) − 1. The mod-4 case is exactly 'total contribution = 1'.

**n = 4 is the trap.** With a = v₂(n) = 2 and no odd prime factor, the 2-part alone contributes (a − 1) = 1, so φ(4) = 2 ≡ 2 (mod 4). This solution has NO odd prime and is therefore invisible to the form 'n = p^k or 2p^k'. `four_is_extra_solution` proves it is genuinely omitted.

**A sum of positive terms equal to 1 is a singleton.** The forward direction rests on the elementary but decisive observation that if every summand is ≥ 1 and the sum is 1, then exactly one summand is present and equals 1 — turning the arithmetic into 'n has a unique odd prime factor', i.e. an odd prime power.

**The parent's guess was doubly imprecise.** The parent sketched 'exactly one odd prime factor to the first power'; in fact the exponent k may be arbitrary (p^k works for all k ≥ 1 since p^(k−1) is odd), and the pure 2-power n = 4 must be added. Both refinements are captured here.

conclusion.summary: The mod-4 refinement of totient parity is settled: φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) — equivalently v₂(φ(n)) = 1 — holds exactly for n ∈ {4} ∪ {p^k, 2p^k : p prime, p ≡ 3 mod 4, k ≥ 1}. 12 theorems, 334 lines, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. The entry corrects the naive form of the characterization by exhibiting n = 4 as an extra solution.
conclusion.implications: The result pins down exactly when the 2-Sylow subgroup of (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ is cyclic of order 2, a clean stepping stone toward the full 2-adic valuation formula (sibling oq-01) and the mod-2^j refinements. Methodologically it shows how a residue-mod-4 question about a multiplicative function collapses, via valuation additivity, to a finite combinatorial statement about prime factors.
openQuestions: Extend to φ(n) ≡ 4 (mod 8) and higher: characterize v₂(φ(n)) = j for each fixed j, i.e. the number of solutions to (v₂(n) − 1) + Σ v₂(p − 1) = j.
Count, asymptotically, the n ≤ X with φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4): the density of {p^k, 2p^k : p ≡ 3 mod 4} plus the single point n = 4.
Give the analogous mod-4 characterization for the Carmichael function λ(n), whose 2-part behaves differently from φ's on 2-power moduli.

sections.title: Module Overview, Imports, and Namespace
sections.summary: Module docstring stating the mod-4 refinement goal, the additive split v₂(φ n) = (a−1) + Σ v₂(p−1), and — prominently — the n = 4 correction: the naive characterization 'n = p^k or 2p^k' is incomplete. Imports `Mathlib` and opens `Nat`/`Finset` (so `φ` is `Nat.totient`).

sections.title: The Arithmetic Core: v₂(m) = 1 ↔ m ≡ 2 (mod 4)
sections.summary: `padicValNat_two_eq_one_iff`: for every natural m, v₂(m) = 1 ↔ m % 4 = 2 (both sides false at m = 0). Proved by squeezing the valuation between the two divisibilities 2 ∣ m and ¬ 4 ∣ m using `padicValNat_dvd_iff_le`, then closing with `omega`. This turns every mod-4 statement below into a valuation statement.

sections.title: Prime-Power Building Blocks
sections.summary: `v2_tot_two_pow` (v₂(φ(2^a)) = a − 1), `v2_tot_odd_prime_pow` (for odd primes, v₂(φ(p^k)) = v₂(p − 1), since p^(k−1) is odd), `v2_pred_eq_one_iff` (v₂(p − 1) = 1 ↔ p ≡ 3 mod 4, via the arithmetic core), and `one_le_v2_pred` (every odd prime contributes ≥ 1 because p − 1 is even).

sections.title: The Odd-Part Valuation as a Sum over Prime Factors
sections.summary: `v2_tot_odd`: for odd m ≠ 0, v₂(φ m) = Σ_{p ∣ m} v₂(p − 1), derived from Euler's product formula and `Nat.factorization_prod`. `v2_tot_odd_eq_one_iff` then characterizes when this sum is 1: since every summand is ≥ 1, the index set must be a singleton, so m = p^k with p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (reconstructed via `isPrimePow_iff_card_primeFactors_eq_one`).

sections.title: The Master Split: Peeling off the Prime 2
sections.summary: `v2_totient_master`: for n ≠ 0, v₂(φ n) = (v₂(n) − 1) + Σ_{p ∣ oddpart} v₂(p − 1). Uses the ordProj/ordCompl decomposition n = 2^(v₂ n)·m (m odd, coprime) with multiplicativity of φ and additivity of v₂ over the product.

sections.title: The Corrected Characterization and the n = 4 Correction
sections.summary: `v2_totient_eq_one_iff` (and its mod-4 form `totient_mod_four_eq_two_iff`): the full biconditional with the three families n = 4, p^k, 2p^k. The forward direction cases on a = v₂(n) ∈ {≤1, =2, ≥3}. `four_is_extra_solution` proves n = 4 satisfies φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) but is neither p^k nor 2p^k for an odd prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4), pinning down the incompleteness of the naive form.

sections.title: Sanity Checks against Small Values
sections.summary: Concrete confirmations via the main theorem and kernel `decide`: n = 3, 4, 6 give v₂(φ) = 1 (φ = 2), while n = 5, 8, 15 give φ ≢ 2 (mod 4) (φ = 4, 4, 8).
